exercises.answer: (a) With \(\cos\phi=0.6\), the real part is \(0.6T_2(x)\) and the imaginary part is the constant \(\sin\phi=0.8\), so \(|P_\phi|^2=0.36T_2^2+0.64\). Measuring would mostly reflect the unwanted constant. (b) The sequence with \(-\phi\) gives \(P_{-\phi}=0.6T_2-0.8i\). An LCU with weights \(\frac12,\frac12\) block-encodes \(\frac12(P_\phi+P_{-\phi})=0.6\,T_2(x)\), the real part alone. (c) The LCU coefficients sum to \(1\), so the subnormalization is \(1\): the encoded number is exactly \(0.6T_2(x)\). The price is one extra ancilla and controlled phase rotations, and the success probability is \(0.36\,T_2(x)^2\). This is the extra-qubit trick the theorem refers to when it promises real targets.

exercises.question: Let \(A=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\\tfrac12&0\end{pmatrix}\). (a) Find its singular values and the input and output directions. (b) Compute \(P^{(SV)}(A)\) for the odd polynomial \(P=T_3\) and the even version \(\sum_jP(\sigma_j)\ket{w_j}\bra{w_j}\) for \(P=T_2\). Which spaces do the two results map between?
exercises.answer: (a) \(A\ket1=1\cdot\ket0\) and \(A\ket0=\frac12\ket1\). So \(\sigma_1=1\) with \(\ket{w_1}=\ket1\), \(\ket{u_1}=\ket0\), and \(\sigma_2=\frac12\) with \(\ket{w_2}=\ket0\), \(\ket{u_2}=\ket1\). (b) For \(T_3\), \(T_3(1)=1\) and \(T_3(\frac12)=4\cdot\frac18-\frac32=-1\), so \(T_3^{(SV)}(A)=\ket0\bra1-\ket1\bra0\). It maps input directions to output directions, like \(A\) itself, with new stretch factors. For \(T_2\), \(T_2(1)=1\) and \(T_2(\frac12)=-\frac12\), giving \(\ket1\bra1-\frac12\ket0\bra0\). It maps the input space to itself, as \(A^\dagger A\) does. The odd transformation changed the singular value \(\frac12\) to magnitude \(1\): QSVT can enlarge singular values, provided the polynomial stays bounded.

exercises.question: For \(\tau=\alpha t=10\), the Jacobi–Anger coefficients are \(J_{10}(10)\approx0.21\), \(J_{15}(10)\approx4.5\times10^{-3}\), \(J_{20}(10)\approx1.2\times10^{-5}\), and \(J_{25}(10)\approx7\times10^{-9}\). (a) Estimate the truncation degree for error \(10^{-6}\) from the rule \(d\approx e\tau/2+\ln(1/\epsilon)\). (b) Using the listed values, judge where the series can actually be cut. (c) How does the degree change if \(\tau\) doubles, or if \(\epsilon\) becomes \(10^{-12}\)?
hints: The tail of the series is dominated by its first omitted coefficient.
The cost is additive in \(\tau\) and \(\log(1/\epsilon)\).
exercises.answer: (a) \(e\cdot10/2+\ln10^6\approx13.6+13.8\approx27\). (b) The coefficients fall from \(0.2\) at \(k=10\) to about \(10^{-5}\) at \(k=20\) and below \(10^{-8}\) at \(k=25\). The tail beyond degree \(22\) or so is already below \(10^{-6}\), so the rule is a safe overestimate. Up to \(k\approx\tau\) the coefficients are not small; beyond it they decay faster than exponentially. (c) Doubling \(\tau\) roughly doubles the degree, because the cutoff sits a little beyond \(k\approx\tau\). Squaring the precision to \(10^{-12}\) adds only a few more terms, because of the super-exponential decay. This is the additive scaling \(O(\alpha t+\log(1/\epsilon))\) in concrete numbers.

exercises.question: A student reasons: “Every QSP response satisfies \(|P(x)|\le1\), so a polynomial transformation can only shrink singular values; it can never turn a small singular value into a large one.” Test this with \(P(x)=3x-4x^3=-T_3(x)\). What does it do to \(x=\frac12\), and which earlier algorithm is this?
exercises.answer: \(P(\frac12)=\frac32-\frac12=1\), so a singular value \(\frac12\) becomes \(1\). On \([-1,1]\), \(P(\sin\theta)=\sin3\theta\), so \(|P|\le1\) everywhere. The bound limits the output, not the ratio of output to input. Near \(0\), \(P(x)\approx3x\), so small values are tripled. Writing the input as \(\sin\theta\), the transformation \(\sin\theta\mapsto\sin3\theta\) is exactly one round of amplitude amplification. Polynomials can amplify small values as long as they stay bounded on the whole interval; boundedness is why the amplification has to slow down near \(1\).

exercises.question: A linear system has κ = 100. Estimate the number of block-encoding calls for the polynomial-inversion algorithm with amplitude amplification, taking the polynomial degree to be κ ln(κ/ε) with ε = 10⁻³, and the amplification count to be κ. Then state what output the algorithm produces.
exercises.answer: Degree ≈ 100 × 11.5 ≈ 1150; amplification needs about 100 rounds, each using the polynomial sequence and its inverse, so about 2 × 1150 × 100 ≈ 2.3 × 10⁵ block-encoding calls (methods with optimal κ log(1/ε) scaling reduce this to about 10³–10⁴). The output is a quantum state proportional to A⁻¹|b⟩, not the vector of solution entries; extracting a classical quantity such as ⟨x|M|x⟩ to precision δ costs further repetitions of order 1/δ with amplitude estimation.

exercises.question: A trial state has overlap \(\gamma=0.1\) with the ground state of \(H\). The block encoding has \(\alpha=100\), the gap is \(\Delta_E=0.5\), and the target error is \(\epsilon=10^{-3}\). Compare, up to constant factors: (a) repeated phase estimation on the qubitized walk, which succeeds with probability \(\gamma^2\) per run and needs about \(\alpha/\Delta_E\) walk steps to resolve the gap; and (b) a spectral filter of degree \((\alpha/\Delta_E)\ln(1/\epsilon)\) combined with amplitude amplification. What does each method output, and which assumption do both share?
exercises.answer: (a) Each run costs about \(\alpha/\Delta_E=200\) walk steps and succeeds with probability \(\gamma^2=0.01\), so about \(100\times200=2\times10^4\) calls are expected (more for high confidence). (b) The filter has degree about \(200\ln10^3\approx1.4\times10^3\). Its success amplitude is about \(\gamma\), so amplitude amplification needs about \(1/\gamma=10\) rounds: about \(1.4\times10^4\) calls. The advantage of (b) grows as \(\gamma\) falls, since \(1/\gamma\) replaces \(1/\gamma^2\). Its \(\ln(1/\epsilon)\) factor is the cost of a sharp filter. Method (a) outputs an energy estimate and a collapsed state; method (b) outputs the ground state coherently, to precision \(\epsilon\), ready for later processing. Both assume a trial state with known nonnegligible overlap and a known gap; neither helps if preparing such a state is the hard part.

09-evolution-engineering.purpose: Engineer time evolution: build e^{−iHt} from short evolutions of simple terms with controlled error, compare simulation strategies fairly, and use slowly changing Hamiltonians to prepare ground states.
09-evolution-engineering.before: Use matrix exponentials and spectral decompositions (Chapter 6), operator-norm error composition (Chapter 3), Pauli-sum block encodings (Chapter 7), and polynomial simulation (Chapter 8).
outcomes: State the simulation problem and the no-fast-forwarding limit.
Compute commutators and explain why noncommuting terms cause product-formula error.
Choose the number of Trotter steps from the first-order bound and compare with actual errors.
Explain how symmetric and higher-order formulas reduce error.
Implement exponentials of Pauli strings with parity circuits and count gates.
Compare product formulas and block-encoding methods under matched assumptions.
Analyze adiabatic evolution through the minimum gap, and state what it does and does not achieve for optimization.
09-evolution-engineering.example: H = X + Z: first-order Trotter with r steps has error about 0.7/r against the bound 1/r, and the adiabatic path from −X to −Z succeeds once the total time is a few units.
09-evolution-engineering.limits: Error bounds are worst-case operator-norm bounds for bounded generators. Hardware noise is not modelled. Adiabatic runtimes depend on gaps that are rarely known for large instances.
09-evolution-engineering.next: Chapter 10 drops guaranteed constructions: it optimizes the parameters of short circuits against measured objectives, and asks what such heuristics can and cannot establish.

exercises.question: For H = Z₁Z₂ + X₁, compute the commutator [Z₁Z₂, X₁] and its norm, and give the first-order step count for t = 2, ε = 0.01.
hints: Z₁ and X₁ anticommute; Z₂ is untouched.
exercises.answer: Z₁Z₂X₁ − X₁Z₁Z₂ = (Z₁X₁ − X₁Z₁)Z₂ = 2iY₁Z₂, with norm 2. So r ≥ 4·2/(2·0.01) = 400 first-order steps by the bound.

exercises.question: Using the rule that Pauli strings commute when they anticommute on an even number of positions, decide which pairs commute among \(X_1X_2\), \(Y_1Y_2\), \(Z_1Z_2\), and \(X_1Z_2\). What is the first-order Trotter error for the Heisenberg pair Hamiltonian \(H=X_1X_2+Y_1Y_2+Z_1Z_2\)?
hints: Compare the strings position by position: distinct non-identity Paulis anticommute.
The first-order bound sums \(\|[H_j,H_k]\|\) over pairs.
exercises.answer: \(X_1X_2\), \(Y_1Y_2\), and \(Z_1Z_2\) differ from each other at both positions, so every pair anticommutes twice and commutes. \(X_1Z_2\) anticommutes once with \(X_1X_2\) (position 2) and once with \(Z_1Z_2\) (position 1), so those pairs anticommute; with \(Y_1Y_2\) it differs at both positions and commutes. For the Heisenberg pair all commutators vanish, so \(e^{-iHt}=e^{-iX_1X_2t}e^{-iY_1Y_2t}e^{-iZ_1Z_2t}\) exactly, with no Trotter error for any \(t\). A single step suffices, which is fast-forwarding. On a chain of many sites, neighbouring bonds share a qubit and do not commute, and the error returns.

exercises.question: For \(H=X+Z\) and target error \(\epsilon=10^{-3}\), how many first-order steps does the commutator bound require at \(t=1\) and at \(t=10\)? How does the second-order formula’s step count, of order \(t^{3/2}/\epsilon^{1/2}\), scale between the same two times?
exercises.answer: The first-order bound needs \(r\ge t^2/\epsilon\): \(1000\) steps at \(t=1\) and \(100\,000\) at \(t=10\), a factor of \(100\) for ten times longer evolution. The second-order count grows by \(10^{3/2}\approx32\). Each first-order step has fixed cost, so the first-order gate count grows as \(t^2\). The no-fast-forwarding theorem requires only linear growth, so the first-order formula pays an extra factor of \(t\). Higher-order formulas, or polynomial methods, close most of that gap.

exercises.question: Write a circuit for e^{−iθ Y₁ Y₂} and count its CNOTs and single-qubit gates.
hints: Map Y to Z with S† followed by H on each qubit.
exercises.answer: On each qubit apply S† then H (mapping Y to Z); CNOT from qubit 1 to qubit 2; R_z(2θ) on qubit 2; CNOT from qubit 1 to 2; then H then S on each qubit. Two CNOTs, one rotation, and eight Clifford single-qubit gates (some of which may cancel with neighbouring terms in a full Trotter step).

exercises.question: For \(H=X+Z\), a single first-order step of length \(\delta=0.1\) has actual error about \(0.00998\), while ten such steps (total time \(1\)) have actual error about \(0.070\). (a) Compare each with the bounds \(\frac{\delta^2}{2}\|[X,Z]\|\) and \(\frac{t^2}{2r}\|[X,Z]\|\). (b) Why is the one-step bound nearly tight while the ten-step bound is loose? (c) Using the actual \(1/r\) scaling, estimate the steps needed for error \(0.01\).
hints: The triangle inequality adds error norms; it ignores directions.
exercises.answer: (a) The one-step bound is \(0.01\cdot2/2=0.01\), matching \(0.00998\) almost exactly. The ten-step bound is \(1\cdot2/20=0.1\), against an actual \(0.070\). (b) For a single short step the leading error term \(-\frac{\delta^2}{2}[X,Z]\) dominates and the bound captures it. Over many steps the bound adds error norms as if every step erred in the worst direction, but the step errors are rotated by the evolution in between and partly cancel, so the total grows more slowly than the sum. (c) The actual error is about \(0.70/r\), so \(r\approx70\) steps reach \(0.01\), against \(100\) from the bound. That difference translates directly into gate count.

exercises.question: Adiabatic search over \(N\) items uses \(H(s)=I-(1-s)\ket u\bra u-s\ket m\bra m\), where \(\ket u\) is the uniform superposition and \(\ket m\) the marked item. For \(N=4\), compute the gap at \(s=0\), \(s=\frac14\), and \(s=\frac12\) using \(g(s)=\sqrt{1-4(1-1/N)s(1-s)}\). Compare the runtimes suggested by the heuristic \(1/g_{\min}^2\) for \(N=4\) and \(N=2^{20}\).
exercises.answer: For \(N=4\): \(g(0)=1\), \(g(\tfrac14)=\sqrt{1-3\cdot\tfrac{3}{16}}=\sqrt{7/16}\approx0.661\), and \(g(\tfrac12)=\sqrt{1-\tfrac34}=\tfrac12=1/\sqrt N\). The heuristic \(1/g_{\min}^2=N\) suggests time of order \(4\) here and \(2^{20}\approx10^6\) for \(N=2^{20}\), no better than classical search. The gap is small only in a window near \(s=\frac12\), of width about \(1/\sqrt N\). A schedule that slows down only there, the local adiabatic schedule, needs time of order \(\sqrt N\approx10^3\), matching Grover search. The improvement comes from knowing where the gap is small.

exercises.question: A first-order simulation has \(L=50\) Pauli terms and \(r=1000\) steps, so \(5\times10^4\) arbitrary rotations. The total error budget is \(10^{-3}\), half allotted to rotation synthesis. Using about \(3\log_2(1/\epsilon_{\mathrm{rot}})\) \(T\) gates per rotation, find \(\epsilon_{\mathrm{rot}}\), the \(T\) count per rotation, and the total \(T\) count. How would halving the number of rotations change the answer?
exercises.answer: The rotation errors add, so \(\epsilon_{\mathrm{rot}}\le5\times10^{-4}/(5\times10^4)=10^{-8}\). Each rotation then costs about \(3\times26.6\approx80\) \(T\) gates, and the total is about \(5\times10^4\times80=4\times10^6\) \(T\) gates. Halving the number of rotations halves the count and also relaxes each rotation’s budget to \(2\times10^{-8}\), saving about \(3\) \(T\) gates per rotation: roughly \(2\times10^6\) in total. The logarithmic dependence means precision is cheap per gate, but the count of rotations, set by \(L\) and \(r\), drives the cost.

exercises.question: A student rescales a Hamiltonian, \(H'=H/10\), and argues that \(e^{-iH't'}\) with \(t'=10t\) equals \(e^{-iHt}\) while every commutator becomes \(100\) times smaller, so Trotterization gets much cheaper. Check the first-order step count and the qubitization cost before and after rescaling.
exercises.answer: For first order, \(r\ge t'^2\|[A',B']\|/(2\epsilon)=(10t)^2\cdot\|[A,B]\|/100/(2\epsilon)=t^2\|[A,B]\|/(2\epsilon)\): unchanged. For qubitization, \(\lambda'=\lambda/10\) and \(\lambda't'=\lambda t\): unchanged. The evolution operator depends only on the product \(Ht\), and so does every honest cost formula. Rescaling changes units, not difficulty. A claimed speedup from “simulating for less time” must be checked against \(\|H\|t\) or \(\lambda t\), the dimensionless quantities the costs depend on.

exercises.question: An adiabatic algorithm for a family of instances has minimum gap g(n) = 1/n² for n qubits. Estimate the runtime with a linear schedule and with a local schedule, and explain whether this would give a polynomial-time algorithm. What would you need to know to trust the gap estimate?
hints: Local schedule: T ~ 1/g in favourable cases.
exercises.answer: Linear: T ~ n⁴; local: T ~ n². Both are polynomial, so if the gap really scales as 1/n² for the whole family, the adiabatic algorithm runs in polynomial time (and can be simulated by a polynomial-size circuit). To trust it, one needs a proof of the gap bound for all instances, or at least strong evidence across sizes, because numerical gaps on small n can miss exponentially small avoided crossings that appear only at larger n.

exercises.question: Derive the gap formula used in adiabatic search. (a) Show that \(H(s)=I-(1-s)\ket u\bra u-s\ket m\bra m\) acts as \(I\) on states orthogonal to both \(\ket u\) and \(\ket m\), so the gap is set by the two-dimensional block they span. (b) In that block, find the trace and determinant of \(M=(1-s)\ket u\bra u+s\ket m\bra m\) using \(|\braket um|^2=1/N\). (c) Deduce \(g(s)=\sqrt{1-4(1-1/N)s(1-s)}\) and its minimum.
hints: For a \(2\times2\) Hermitian matrix the eigenvalue difference is \(\sqrt{(\mathrm{tr})^2-4\det}\).
exercises.answer: (a) A state orthogonal to \(\ket u\) and \(\ket m\) is annihilated by both projectors, so \(H(s)\) gives eigenvalue \(1\). The other eigenvalues live in the span of \(\ket u,\ket m\), where \(H=I-M\). (b) \(\mathrm{tr}M=(1-s)+s=1\). For the determinant, write \(M\) in an orthonormal basis \(\{\ket m,\ket{m^\perp}\}\) with \(\ket u=\frac{1}{\sqrt N}\ket m+\sqrt{1-\frac1N}\ket{m^\perp}\); a direct calculation gives \(\det M=s(1-s)(1-\frac1N)\). (c) The eigenvalues of \(M\) differ by \(\sqrt{1-4s(1-s)(1-\frac1N)}\), and so do those of \(H=I-M\). The smaller eigenvalue of \(H\), \(\frac12(1-\sqrt{\cdots})\), is the ground energy. The larger, \(\frac12(1+\sqrt{\cdots})\le1\), is the first excited energy, below the eigenvalue \(1\) of the orthogonal states. So the gap is \(g(s)=\sqrt{1-4(1-1/N)s(1-s)}\), minimized at \(s=\frac12\) with \(g_{\min}=1/\sqrt N\).

10-variational-methods.purpose: Understand variational algorithms as heuristics: parameterized circuits, measured objectives, classical optimization, and the evidence needed to judge their performance.
10-variational-methods.before: Use expectation values, Pauli decompositions and the 1-norm (Chapter 7), measurement statistics (Chapter 1), and adiabatic evolution (Chapter 9).
outcomes: Describe an ansatz and the trade-off between expressiveness and cost.
Estimate an energy from Pauli measurements and compute shot budgets with optimal allocation.
Derive and apply the parameter-shift rule.
Distinguish shot noise from hardware bias and explain barren plateaus.
State the variational principle and its overlap consequence, and the three gaps in a variational eigensolver result.
Compute a depth-1 QAOA example and explain the role of the mixer.
List the evidence required to support claims about heuristic quantum algorithms.
10-variational-methods.example: The two-qubit ansatz cos(θ/2)|00⟩ + sin(θ/2)|11⟩ minimizing E(θ) = −1 − sin θ for H = −ZZ − XX, and depth-1 QAOA on a single edge with expected cut ½ + ½ sin 4β sin γ.
10-variational-methods.limits: Calculations are noiseless unless stated. Variational methods carry no general performance guarantee; the stated QAOA approximation ratio is a cited result for a specific graph class.
10-variational-methods.next: Chapter 11 brings measurement inside the computation: mid-circuit outcomes control later operations, trade coherent resources for classical feedback, and drive measurement-based computation.

exercises.question: For the ansatz cos(θ/2)|00⟩ + sin(θ/2)|11⟩, compute ⟨Z₁⟩ and ⟨Z₁Z₂⟩ as functions of θ.
exercises.answer: ⟨Z₁⟩ = cos²(θ/2) − sin²(θ/2) = cos θ, and ⟨Z₁Z₂⟩ = 1 for every θ. So a Hamiltonian H = −Z₁ would have E(θ) = −cos θ, minimized at θ = 0 (the state |00⟩).

exercises.question: In the running example at \(\theta=\pi/6\), \(\langle X_1X_2\rangle=\sin\theta=\frac12\). Find the variance of one \(\pm1\) shot of \(X_1X_2\) and the standard deviation of the average of \(1000\) shots. Why does \(\langle Z_1Z_2\rangle\) need no shots at all for this ansatz?
hints: A \(\pm1\) outcome with mean \(\mu\) has variance \(1-\mu^2\).
Every state in the family is supported on \(\ket{00}\) and \(\ket{11}\).
exercises.answer: The single-shot variance is \(1-\frac14=\frac34\), so \(1000\) shots give standard deviation \(\sqrt{0.75/1000}\approx0.027\). Every trial state is a combination of \(\ket{00}\) and \(\ket{11}\), both with \(Z_1Z_2=+1\), so every shot returns \(+1\). The variance is \(0\) and \(\langle Z_1Z_2\rangle=1\) is known exactly. Variances depend on the state, which is why the optimal shot allocation \(R_j\propto|h_j|\sigma_j\) can save far more than the worst-case bound \(\lambda^2/\epsilon^2\) suggests.

exercises.question: For depth-1 QAOA on a single edge, set \(\gamma=\pi\). Compute the state after the cost layer, starting from \(\ket{++}\), and explain why no mixer angle \(\beta\) can then improve the expected cut beyond \(\frac12\). Compare with the formula \(F=\frac12+\frac12\sin4\beta\sin\gamma\).
hints: \(C\) is \(1\) on \(01\) and \(10\), so \(e^{-i\pi C}\) multiplies those components by \(-1\).
exercises.answer: After the cost layer the state is \(\frac12(\ket{00}-\ket{01}-\ket{10}+\ket{11})=\ket-\ket-\). That is an eigenstate of \(X_1+X_2\) (eigenvalue \(-2\)), so the mixer only multiplies it by a global phase. The measured distribution stays uniform, with expected cut \(\frac12\) for every \(\beta\). The formula agrees: \(\sin\pi=0\). The cost phases \(e^{-i\gamma C}\) must create relative phases that the mixer can turn into probability differences; at \(\gamma=\pi\) the phases form a pattern the mixer cannot use.

exercises.question: Use the parameter-shift rule to compute the gradient of E(θ) = −1 − sin θ at θ = π/3, and take one gradient-descent step with η = 0.5.
exercises.answer: E(π/3 + π/2) = −1 − cos(π/3) = −1.5 and E(π/3 − π/2) = −1 + cos(π/3) = −0.5, so dE/dθ = (−1.5 + 0.5)/2 = −0.5 = −cos(π/3). The step gives θ = π/3 + 0.25 ≈ 1.297, closer to the optimum π/2 ≈ 1.571; the energy falls from −1.866 to about −1.963.

exercises.question: Add a field to the example: \(H=-Z_1Z_2-X_1X_2+0.5\,Z_1\). (a) Show that for the ansatz \(\cos\frac\theta2\ket{00}+\sin\frac\theta2\ket{11}\), \(E(\theta)=-1-\sin\theta+0.5\cos\theta\). (b) Find the minimum and its location. (c) Show that \(H\) maps the span of \(\ket{00},\ket{11}\) to itself and find its lowest eigenvalue there. Does the ansatz contain the ground state?
exercises.answer: (a) As before \(\langle Z_1Z_2\rangle=1\) and \(\langle X_1X_2\rangle=\sin\theta\), and \(\langle Z_1\rangle=\cos\theta\), giving \(E=-1-\sin\theta+0.5\cos\theta\). (b) \(E=-1-\sqrt{1.25}\sin(\theta-\varphi)\) with \(\varphi=\arctan0.5\approx0.464\). The minimum is \(-1-\sqrt{1.25}\approx-2.118\) at \(\theta=\pi/2+\varphi\approx2.03\). (c) Each term maps \(\ket{00}\) and \(\ket{11}\) into their span. In the basis \((\ket{00},\ket{11})\), \(H=\begin{pmatrix}-0.5&-1\\-1&-1.5\end{pmatrix}\), with eigenvalues \(-1\pm\sqrt{1.25}\). The odd sector \(\{\ket{01},\ket{10}\}\) has eigenvalues \(1\pm\sqrt{1.25}\), the lowest being \(-0.118\). So the true ground energy is \(-2.118\), and the ansatz attains it. It succeeds because it covers every real state in the symmetry sector that contains the ground state. Without that structure, the family could easily miss the ground state.

exercises.question: A variational run reports energy \(-1.95\) for a Hamiltonian with \(E_0=-2\). (a) If every excited energy is at least \(0\) (gap \(\Delta=2\)), bound the ground-state overlap \(|c_0|^2\). (b) Repeat for a gap \(\Delta=0.1\). (c) An observable \(O\) with \(\|O\|\le1\) is computed from the variational state. Using \(|c_0|^2\), roughly how far can its value be from the ground-state value in each case?
hints: A state with overlap \(|c_0|^2\) has trace distance about \(\sqrt{1-|c_0|^2}\) from the ground state.
exercises.answer: (a) \(|c_0|^2\ge1-0.05/2=0.975\). (b) \(|c_0|^2\ge1-0.05/0.1=0.5\), so up to half the weight may lie on excited states. (c) For a pure state, the distance from the ground state is \(\sqrt{1-|c_0|^2}\). This is at most about \(0.16\) in case (a) and up to about \(0.71\) in case (b), and expectation values of \(O\) can be off by twice that. The same energy error means very different things depending on the gap. A small gap makes energy a poor certificate of the state, so a reported variational energy does not validate other computed properties unless a gap bound is known.

exercises.question: Verify the depth-1 QAOA formula for one edge at \(\gamma=\pi/2\) by working in the two-dimensional space spanned by \(\ket{\Phi^+}=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}(\ket{00}+\ket{11})\) and \(\ket{\Psi^+}=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}(\ket{01}+\ket{10})\). (a) Write the state after the cost layer in this basis. (b) Show that \(B=X_1+X_2\) acts as \(2\sigma_x\) there. (c) Compute the probability of an uncut outcome and the expected cut as a function of \(\beta\).
exercises.answer: (a) \(\ket{++}=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}(\ket{\Phi^+}+\ket{\Psi^+})\); after the cost layer it is \(\frac{1}{\sqrt2}(\ket{\Phi^+}-i\ket{\Psi^+})\). (b) \(X_1+X_2\) sends \(\ket{00}+\ket{11}\) to \(2(\ket{01}+\ket{10})\), so \(B\ket{\Phi^+}=2\ket{\Psi^+}\) and \(B\ket{\Psi^+}=2\ket{\Phi^+}\). (c) Applying \(\cos2\beta\,I-i\sin2\beta\,\sigma_x\) gives the \(\ket{\Phi^+}\) amplitude \(\frac{1}{\sqrt2}(\cos2\beta-\sin2\beta)\). The uncut probability is \(\frac12(\cos2\beta-\sin2\beta)^2=\frac12(1-\sin4\beta)\), so the expected cut is \(F=\frac12(1+\sin4\beta)\), matching the formula with \(\sin\gamma=1\). At \(\beta=\pi/8\) the uncut amplitude vanishes and \(F=1\). The symmetry of the problem reduced a four-dimensional calculation to a rotation in a plane.

exercises.question: An optimizer for \(E(\theta)=-1-\sin\theta\) starts at \(\theta_0=3\pi/2\), computes an exact gradient of zero, and stops, reporting convergence. What has it found? What would happen with shot noise, and what does this say about using a zero gradient as a certificate?
exercises.answer: \(E(3\pi/2)=-1+1=0\), the maximum of the landscape, not the minimum \(-2\) at \(\theta=\pi/2\). The gradient vanishes at every stationary point: minima, maxima, and saddles. With shot noise the estimated gradient would be slightly nonzero, and the optimizer would drift away from this unstable point, so noise happens to help here. In larger landscapes, local minima are stable and noise does not rescue the run. A small gradient shows only that the optimizer has stopped moving. It says nothing about global optimality, and in a barren plateau it may simply reflect a landscape too flat to measure.

exercises.question: A Hamiltonian has λ = 20, and each optimizer iteration estimates the energy and a 50-component gradient by parameter shift, each energy to precision 10⁻². Estimate the shots per iteration, and comment on 500 iterations.
hints: Each energy estimate needs about λ²/ε² shots.
A gradient by parameter shift needs 2 × 50 energy estimates (with the same precision per component as a rough guide).
exercises.answer: One energy: 400/10⁻⁴ = 4 × 10⁶ shots. Gradient: 100 energies, 4 × 10⁸ shots. Per iteration about 4 × 10⁸ shots; 500 iterations need about 2 × 10¹¹ shots. At 10⁴ shots per second that is about 230 days, illustrating why measurement cost dominates variational methods and why shot-frugal optimizers and measurement grouping matter.

exercises.question: For \(H=-Z_1Z_2-X_1X_2\) at \(\theta=\pi/3\), use the optimal allocation \(R_j\propto|h_j|\sigma_j\). (a) Compute \(\sigma_1,\sigma_2\) and the shots needed for standard error \(10^{-3}\) in the energy. (b) Compare with the worst-case estimate \(\lambda^2/\epsilon^2\). (c) The allocation uses the very expectation values being estimated. Propose a practical procedure, and say what it costs.
exercises.answer: (a) \(\sigma_1=\sqrt{1-1}=0\) and \(\sigma_2=\sqrt{1-0.75}=0.5\). The optimal allocation gives all shots to \(X_1X_2\), and \(\mathrm{Var}=(0.5)^2/R\). Standard error \(10^{-3}\) needs \(R=0.25/10^{-6}=2.5\times10^5\) shots. (b) The worst case \(\lambda^2/\epsilon^2=4/10^{-6}=4\times10^6\) is sixteen times larger. (c) Spend a small pilot budget on every term to estimate each \(\sigma_j\), then allocate the remaining shots proportionally to \(|h_j|\hat\sigma_j\), keeping a minimum for every term in case a pilot estimate was misleading. The pilot costs a modest fraction of the total. Since \(\sigma_j\) changes slowly as \(\theta\) moves during optimization, earlier estimates can be reused.

11-adaptive-measurement.purpose: Use measurement inside a computation: branch on outcomes, defer or advance measurements, estimate phases adaptively with one qubit, and compute by measurement with teleported gates and injected magic states.
11-adaptive-measurement.before: Use phase estimation and the inverse QFT (Chapter 4), the Hadamard test (Chapter 3), postselection (Chapter 7), and gate costs in Clifford+T (Chapter 2).
outcomes: Track branch probabilities, conditional states, and classical records through mid-circuit measurements.
Apply the deferred measurement principle in both directions and compare the resources.
Construct measurement-dependent Pauli corrections and analyze repeat-until-success costs.
Run iterative phase estimation with feedback and explain the semiclassical Fourier transform.
Distinguish the standard quantum limit from the Heisenberg limit.
Derive one-bit gate teleportation and the angle adaptation in measurement-based computation.
Explain magic-state injection and why distillation dominates fault-tolerant costs.
11-adaptive-measurement.example: Iterative estimation of φ = 3/8 with one control qubit and two classical corrections, and T-gate injection from the magic state T|+⟩ with a single CNOT, measurement, and conditional S.
11-adaptive-measurement.limits: Measurements are ideal and feedback is instantaneous unless stated. The iterative-estimation analysis assumes an exact eigenstate and exactly representable phases; general phases need repetition and statistical processing.
11-adaptive-measurement.next: This completes the technique sequence. The Quantum Programming course turns these constructions into executable circuits, with tests that check contracts, amplitudes, and resource counts.

exercises.question: In one-bit teleportation with α = π/2, what gate is applied (after correcting the byproduct)?
exercises.answer: HP(−π/2) = HS†. On outcome 1, apply X to remove the byproduct; the auxiliary qubit then holds HS†|ψ⟩.

exercises.question: Prepare \(\frac{1}{\sqrt2}(\ket{00}+\ket{11})\) and measure the first qubit in the \(\{\ket+,\ket-\}\) basis. What is the second qubit’s state for each outcome, and which feedforward correction makes it \(\ket+\) in both cases?
exercises.answer: Since \(\frac{1}{\sqrt2}(\ket{00}+\ket{11})=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}(\ket{++}+\ket{--})\), outcome \(+\) leaves the second qubit in \(\ket+\) and outcome \(-\) leaves \(\ket-\), each with probability \(\frac12\). Applying \(Z\) after outcome \(-\) gives \(\ket+\) deterministically. The choice of measurement basis determines which states the partner can be steered to; the correction is a Pauli gate chosen by the record.

exercises.question: A qubit carries a pending Pauli byproduct \(X\) in the Pauli frame. The program then applies \(H\) and \(S\), and measures in the computational basis. How does the byproduct propagate, and must the measured bit be flipped? What if no \(H\) had been applied?
hints: A \(Z\) just before a computational-basis measurement does not change the outcome.
exercises.answer: Moving the byproduct through the gates: \(SHX=SZH=ZSH\), so just before the measurement the frame holds \(Z\). A \(Z\) does not change computational-basis probabilities, so the measured bit is reported unchanged. Without the \(H\), \(SX=YS\), and \(Y=iXZ\) contains an \(X\), which flips a computational-basis outcome, so the classical controller must invert the measured bit. Tracking the frame lets the hardware skip the correction gates; only the interpretation of later outcomes changes.

exercises.question: Run iterative phase estimation for φ = 7/8 = 0.111 in binary, giving each stage’s phase, correction, and outcome.
hints: Stage 3 uses U⁴, stage 2 uses U², stage 1 uses U.
The correction at stage k is 2π(0.0 b_{k+1} … b_m).
exercises.answer: Stage 3: phase 2π·(28/8) ≡ 2π·½, no correction, b₃ = 1. Stage 2: phase 2π·(14/8) ≡ 2π·¾, subtract 2π·¼, leaving π: b₂ = 1. Stage 1: phase 2π·⅞, subtract 2π·(0.011)₂ = 2π·⅜, leaving 2π·½ = π: b₁ = 1. Result 0.111 = 7/8.

exercises.question: Run two-stage iterative phase estimation on an eigenstate with \(\phi=1/3\), which has no finite binary expansion. (a) Compute the probability of each outcome at stage 2 (controlled-\(U^2\), no correction). (b) For each stage-2 outcome, apply the correction \(P(-\omega_1)\) with \(\omega_1=2\pi(0.0b_2)\) and compute the stage-1 probabilities. (c) Tabulate the probabilities of the four estimates \(0.b_1b_2\) and compare them with textbook phase estimation with \(M=4\).
exercises.answer: (a) Stage 2 sees phase \(4\pi/3\), so \(\Pr[b_2=0]=(1+\cos\frac{4\pi}{3})/2=\frac14\) and \(\Pr[b_2=1]=\frac34\). (b) If \(b_2=0\), there is no correction and stage 1 sees \(2\pi/3\): \(\Pr[b_1=0]=\frac14\). If \(b_2=1\), \(\omega_1=\pi/2\) and stage 1 sees \(2\pi/3-\pi/2=\pi/6\): \(\Pr[b_1=0]=(1+\cos\frac\pi6)/2\approx0.933\). (c) The estimates \(0.00,0.01,0.10,0.11\) (that is \(0,\frac14,\frac12,\frac34\)) have probabilities \(\frac14\cdot\frac14=0.0625\), \(\frac34\times0.933\approx0.700\), \(\frac14\cdot\frac34=0.1875\), and \(\frac34\times0.067\approx0.050\). Textbook phase estimation with \(M=4\) gives exactly the same four numbers. The two procedures are related by deferred measurement, so their output statistics agree even when the phase is not exact.

exercises.question: In teleportation, the state just before Alice measures is \(\frac12\sum_{m_1,m_2}\ket{m_1m_2}\,X^{m_2}Z^{m_1}\ket\psi\). Apply the deferred-measurement principle: replace the classically controlled corrections by a CNOT from Alice’s second qubit and a controlled-\(Z\) from her first qubit to Bob’s. Find the final three-qubit state, and explain what Alice’s later measurements reveal.
hints: The correction must undo \(X^{m_2}Z^{m_1}\): apply \(X^{m_2}\) first, then \(Z^{m_1}\).
exercises.answer: On the branch \(\ket{m_1m_2}\), the controlled gates apply \(Z^{m_1}X^{m_2}\) to Bob’s qubit, turning \(X^{m_2}Z^{m_1}\ket\psi\) into \(\ket\psi\). The final state is \(\frac12\sum_{m_1,m_2}\ket{m_1m_2}\ket\psi=\ket+\ket+\ket\psi\). Bob holds \(\ket\psi\), unentangled with Alice, and Alice’s qubits are in a fixed state that carries no information about \(\psi\). Measuring them gives two uniformly random bits. The deferred version gives the same statistics as the original, but it needs quantum control from Alice’s qubits to Bob’s, so it is no longer a protocol between distant parties. Classical communication is what lets teleportation work at a distance.

exercises.question: On a three-qubit line cluster, the input sits on qubit 1. Measuring qubit 1 with angle \(\alpha_1\) and qubit 2 with angle \(\alpha_2\) applies \(X^{m_2}HP(-\alpha_2)X^{m_1}HP(-\alpha_1)\) to the input, which ends on qubit 3. (a) Choose \(\alpha_1,\alpha_2\) to apply \(T\), up to byproducts, when both outcomes are \(0\). (b) For \(m_1=1\), \(m_2=0\), find the byproduct on the output and say whether the second angle needs adapting.
exercises.answer: (a) With \(\alpha_2=0\), the composite is \(HHP(-\alpha_1)=P(-\alpha_1)\). Choosing \(\alpha_1=-\pi/4\) gives \(P(\pi/4)=T\). (b) With \(m_1=1\), the operation is \(HP(0)XHT=HXHT=ZT\), so the output is \(ZT\ket\psi\). A \(Z\) byproduct is recorded in the Pauli frame and corrected later, or absorbed into the interpretation of a final measurement. Because \(\alpha_2=0\), flipping its sign changes nothing, so no adaptation is needed here. For a general \(\alpha_2\), the outcome \(m_1=1\) would require measuring with \(-\alpha_2\) instead, since \(P(\beta)X=e^{i\beta}XP(-\beta)\).

exercises.question: A student writes: “Iterative phase estimation uses one control qubit and \(m\) measurements, so it needs only \(m\) applications of controlled-\(U\) instead of \(2^m-1\).” Correct the claim, state what iterative phase estimation actually saves, and say when the number of controlled-\(U\) applications really is small.
hints: Compare the cost of \(U^{2^j}\) for modular multiplication and for \(e^{-iHt}\).
exercises.answer: Stage \(k\) applies controlled-\(U^{2^{k-1}}\). Built from repeated controlled-\(U\), the stages cost \(1+2+\cdots+2^{m-1}=2^m-1\) applications in total, exactly as in the textbook circuit. Iterative estimation saves width: one recycled control qubit instead of \(m\), and no coherent inverse QFT. It also shortens the required coherence time of the control. The count of controlled powers is small only when \(U^{2^j}\) has a shortcut, as for modular multiplication, where \(U_a^{2^j}=U_{a^{2^j}\bmod L}\) costs the same as \(U_a\). For Hamiltonian evolution there is generally no such shortcut, and the total evolution time grows as \(2^m\), as the Heisenberg limit requires.

exercises.question: A fault-tolerant algorithm needs 10⁸ T gates with total failure probability below 1%. Raw magic states have error 10⁻³, and the 15-to-1 protocol maps error p to 35p³. How many rounds of distillation are needed, and roughly how many raw magic states per T gate?
hints: Each T gate may fail with probability at most about 10⁻¹⁰.
One round gives 3.5 × 10⁻⁸; two rounds give about 1.5 × 10⁻²¹.
exercises.answer: Per-gate error must be below about 10⁻²/10⁸ = 10⁻¹⁰. One round gives 3.5 × 10⁻⁸, not enough; two rounds give about 1.5 × 10⁻²¹, more than enough. Two rounds consume about 15² = 225 raw states per output T gate (more with failed rounds), so about 2 × 10¹⁰ raw magic states in total. In practice protocols are mixed and tuned to avoid overshooting the target, which is why T counts dominate resource estimates.

exercises.question: A circuit contains \(10^6\) repeat-until-success gadgets, each succeeding with probability \(p=3/4\) per attempt, all running in parallel. (a) What is the expected total number of attempts? (b) For one gadget, how many attempts guarantee success with probability \(1-10^{-9}\)? (c) Roughly how many attempts does the slowest of the \(10^6\) gadgets typically need, and why does this matter for scheduling?
hints: One gadget needs more than \(k\) attempts with probability \((1-p)^k=4^{-k}\).
The slowest of \(G\) gadgets exceeds \(k\) attempts with probability about \(G\cdot4^{-k}\).
exercises.answer: (a) Each gadget needs \(1/p=4/3\) attempts on average, so about \(1.33\times10^6\) attempts in total, which is the quantity that sets the expected \(T\) count. (b) \(4^{-k}\le10^{-9}\) needs \(k\ge9\log_410\approx15\) attempts. (c) The slowest gadget exceeds \(k\) attempts with probability about \(10^6\cdot4^{-k}\), which is of order one at \(k\approx\log_410^6\approx10\). So the slowest gadget typically needs about \(10\) attempts, although the average is \(1.33\). If later gates must wait for all gadgets, latency is set by this maximum, not the mean, and idle qubits decohere while they wait. Resource estimates for adaptive circuits should therefore report latency or depth separately from expected gate counts.
